items.summary: Los Angeles Unified School District quietly disabled AI Overview in Google searches on school-issued devices, making it the largest district to sideline Google's artificial intelligence features. The move was confirmed after Schools Beyond Screens LA collected videos from parents showing that AI Overview no longer appeared in search results and then contacted the district directly. Los Angeles Unified School District said it temporarily suspended AI Overview to ensure student experiences were age-appropriate and safe, though officials provided no further details on how or for how long the feature would remain disabled.
items.title: Los Angeles School District Disables Google AI Search Feature

items.summary:
An Indian court declined on Nov 27 to halt a Tata Sons board meeting scheduled for Nov 30, which is set to discuss steps toward a central bank-mandated stock market listing. The Reserve Bank of India had told Tata Sons in November that it must comply with the rule requiring its shares be listed, intensifying pressure on the holding company of the salt-to-software conglomerate after more than a century as a private entity.

The meeting will also address reappointing N. Chandrasekaran as chairman, a decision that has created a public rift between Tata Sons and its controlling charities led by family patriarch Noel Tata. The trusts challenged Chandrasekaran's reappointment in the high court in Mumbai this week, arguing under internal governance rules that he should not have been appointed without consent from both nominee directors, including Noel Tata. Abhishek Manu Singhvi, lawyer for the Tata Trusts, warned that allowing the meeting to proceed could set a precedent that Noel Tata's rights as a trust nominee are not honored.

Tata Sons opposed halting the board meeting, stating the listing is mandated by the central bank and must be informed of the company's plans by Dec 11. The company's lawyer Harish Salve argued that internal rules cannot stall the functioning of the company. Two of the seven charities controlling the group filed challenges against Chandrasekaran's reappointment, while the court will next take up the case in January.
items.title: Indian Court Allows Tata Sons Board Meeting on Listing to Proceed

items.summary:
Budget carrier Norse Atlantic announced on Nov 27 that it would file a bankruptcy petition for its main Norwegian operating unit, halting ticket sales and cancelling all flights. The company cited an inability to secure sufficient funding to meet short-term liquidity needs, with the board filing with the Agder District Court in Norway.

Norse becomes the second European airline to enter bankruptcy proceedings in 2026 after Latvia's airBaltic, according to Norse itself. The collapse is attributed by the company and analysts to fuel-cost spikes stemming from the war between Iran and the United States that began at the end of February, which pushed jet fuel prices higher for carriers lacking fuel hedges.

On Nov 25 Norse described its financial situation as 'critical,' then suspended all flights on Nov 26. On Nov 27 it said lessors had terminated leasing contracts for all 12 aircraft in its fleet and demanded the planes be returned, a claim the company contests. The leases were signed in 2021: nine Boeing 787 Dreamliners from AerCap Holdings running about 12 years each, and six Dreamliners from BOC Aviation running 16 years.

Aviation analyst John Strickland said that although Norse is contesting the termination notices, 'it sounds pretty decisive,' adding that unless successful they will not be able to resume operations. The company has advised passengers against going to airports, noted refunds could be claimed in insolvency without guarantee of payment, and reported 1,071 employees as at June 30.

Founded in 2021 by Bjorn Tore Larsen, Norse sought to revive budget transatlantic flights but lacked feeder regional service that analysts warned would hamper load factors. It later diversified into charter and aircraft leasing services while struggling with profits from scheduled flights alone.
items.title: Norse Atlantic's Norwegian Unit Declares Bankruptcy

items.summary:
Microsoft announced at the Ignite 2026 conference that its next major server operating system, Windows Server 2028, will remove the WSUS (Windows Server Update Services) server role entirely. The tool was introduced in 2005 as Software Update Services and lets IT administrators centrally manage and distribute Microsoft updates across corporate networks with many Windows devices instead of letting each device download them individually.

Microsoft had already officially deprecated WSUS in September 2024 while promising to keep it functional through the update channel, but a recently updated support document now confirms that Windows Server 2028 strips out the server role altogether. The change affects enterprise environments relying on WSUS for managing updates across many devices and does not impact home users or those using Microsoft Configuration Manager; WSUS remains available in earlier releases such as Windows Server 2025 through each release's support lifecycle.

Microsoft recommends that organizations transition to cloud-based solutions like Windows Autopatch, Microsoft Intune, and Azure Update Manager. Nir Froimovici of Microsoft stated in September 2024 that while the WSUS role remains available in Windows Server 2025, it is no longer being invested with new features.

Windows Server 2028 also removes VBScript, which was disabled by default in Internet Explorer 11 on Windows 10, and the legacy WMIC utility, deprecated in Windows Server 2012 and Windows 10 version 21H1. WINS support, deprecated with Windows Server 2022's August 2021 release, is likewise being removed.

The operating system can be tested by registering for the Windows Insider Program for Windows Server or applying to enroll in the Windows Server Technology Adoption Program.
items.title: Microsoft to Remove WSUS Server Role in Windows Server 2028

The author tested video generation on an AWS Trainium3 machine (trn3.48xlarge, 64 NeuronCores) for a month spent mostly evaluating Hugging Face models, then used five remaining days to try generating videos with LTX-2.5 from Lightricks.

Once the models were loaded, a 10-second clip with sound took 22 to 23 seconds on half of the machine at 2048x1024 resolution (ev2, ev9, dt10). The author set aside CUDA because no comparable figure existed and instead compared against LTX's online API, which claims a 10-second 1080p clip in 23.7 seconds per LTX (ev6, ev7); the local setup matched that claim and beat it by about a second.

The author had two goals: assessing how easy video generation is with diffusers on Trainium3 for short films from scripts rather than simple example clips, and matching CUDA or LTX's API performance. The input was a JSON list of shots each with a name and prompt resembling a storyboard (ev12), where chaining via 'from' and 'to' keys keeps subjects consistent across cuts by starting or ending on frames of other shots.

The author built the seal film pose to pose, treating the iceberg shot as the payoff that earlier shots lead into. Three diffusers pipelines share LTX-2.5's models: two follow an 8-step then third-pipeline recipe with a latent upsampler adding three final steps (ev19, ev20), and about 160 lines of Python assemble the film on top.

Out of the box the model did not run on NeuronCores because the transformer does not fit on one core. Getting it working required tensor parallelism across cores due to memory limits capped at 32 attention heads, sequence parallelism to use all 64 cores and enable 2048x1024 resolution, and host-side fixes that cut a clip's host time from about 280 seconds to about 8 seconds (roughly 35 times) while device compute fell from 45 seconds to 15 seconds.

The author noted unresolved issues including NaN results at certain sizes when the transformer compiled as one graph, slow first shots ending on keyframes in new processes, and a latent upsampler that fails to load next to the transformer. Some fixes are being handled upstream through open diffusers issues (ev22, ev23), with tensor and context parallelism consolidation planned.

On features, each shot stays consistent by chaining frames rather than prompts alone, takes differ by seed so several can be generated and one selected, and re-running the same code yields a byte-for-byte identical film. Limitations include details getting wrong requiring multiple takes per shot (the goat produced funny horns in 3 of 4 takes), sound not carrying over between shots beyond background leveling, and each shot lasting at most 20 seconds.

The author also applied LTX-2.5 to real footage from a humanoid robot head camera and a car front camera in a snowstorm, letting the model invent what happens after seeing only the first second of a clip. This produced not just one continuation but a distribution of takes reproducible by film file and seed, which could help train robots on rare or risky events too difficult to film.

The author concluded that while LTX-2.5 can draft films and generate plausible continuations from real footage, training setups would need generation conditioned on the robot's or car's actual actions rather than prompts alone.
items.title: Taking Trainium3 to the Track

Dinesh Rai, an emergency physician who taught himself coding before medical school and completed a clinical informatics fellowship, joined Boston Children's Hospital as its first-ever prompt engineer in August 2023 after applying to the hospital's 2023 job listing. Three years later he still works there but describes his role as that of a broader 'clinical AI engineer,' since better models have made elaborate prompting less central and shifted focus toward embedding tools into daily operations, building agents, and determining whether outputs can be trusted, according to John Brownstein, the hospital's chief innovation officer.

Rai splits roughly half his day between writing code with developers and spending time with clinicians to understand their needs. His clinical doppelgangers project helps doctors treating rare or complex patients find similar historical cases for reference rather than as a substitute for randomized trials, illustrating that such work requires understanding hospital data, how clinicians will use answers, and where systems can fail.

In one collaboration over deciding what portion of a patient's record to give an AI model, Rai found both developers—who assumed any data point could help—and clinicians—who assumed the model would ignore irrelevant findings—were wrong. He noted that clinically an abnormal lab result or vital sign may not matter for a given question, and technically an LLM cannot be relied on to recognize irrelevance; it might instead construct a plausible explanation even when the record does not support one.

On reliability, Rai's team had clinicians review generated clinical notes before finalizing them, trusting that someone who cared for a patient over weeks would catch errors more readily than someone skimming afterward. He said some skepticism about AI is healthy and should not be dismissed, noting people trust tools more after seeing their mistakes than when told they are good.

Rai cautioned against telling aspiring engineers to master any specific tool; he emphasized that fundamental programming skills remain valuable for hands-on roles, as does machine learning knowledge and experience building systems. He identified domain knowledge—understanding how health care workflows operate, how electronic health record data is created and what it represents, and where care breaks down—as indispensable.

He concluded that the durable value lies not in extracting answers from a model but in knowing what context it needs and whether that context supports the answer being sought.
items.title: ER Physician Dinesh Rai Becomes Boston Children's First Clinical AI Engineer

Sarah Wynn-Williams, former director of global public policy at Meta and author of a memoir alleging the company collaborated with the Chinese government on censorship tools and harmed teenagers, called on Prime Minister Andy Burnham to strengthen his ban on non-disclosure agreements. Speaking at London's annual Orwell lecture, she said NDAs had become 'a key weapon used by the powerful to keep control over narrative,' arguing their aim is not to win an argument but to leave no record or contestable standard of truth against which those in power can be measured.

Wynn-Williams welcomed Burnham's earlier commitment to ensure victims of crimes or workplace harassment retain freedom to speak even after signing an NDA, but urged him to make the changes retrospective and called on the public to lobby MPs for stronger action. She compared NDAs to Orwell's 'memory hole' from 1984, warning that insiders who developed artificial intelligence are especially at risk because they must sign away their rights to speak in order to work inside the industry.

The whistleblower said she could not discuss her own allegations due to restrictions secured by Meta through a severance agreement and an interim arbitration ruling. She is suing the company over those limitations, sat silent on stage earlier this year after taking legal advice at the Hay literary festival, and noted that NDAs are signed across all levels of employment from executives to gig workers. Meta disputes her book as containing false claims and described her legal case as a ploy to shift more copies.

Wynn-Williams argued that technology companies have learned 'to buy silence by contract,' with courts enforcing those agreements, yet society relies on silenced insiders to warn about AI's most dangerous developments. She said NDAs are signed at moments of maximum vulnerability and can be used to stop anyone from blowing the whistle.
items.title: Meta Whistleblower Urges Burnham to Extend NDA Ban

Elon Musk says Tesla’s next-generation AI5 chip is going to the Optimus robot rather than its cars because current hardware already handles superhuman driving. A report from Taiwan's Commercial Times offers a more practical explanation: Tesla will lack enough AI5 chips for its car fleet until 2028, so it is prioritizing low-volume products.

According to that report, chip design partner Global Unichip (GUC) is allocating TSMC’s limited 3nm capacity in 2027 first to Google and Microsoft data center projects like Axion 2 and Axion 3. The supply chain says Tesla's initial 2027 wafer quota cannot support annual shipments for a fleet of millions of cars, so the scarce volume goes first to Optimus, which ships in small numbers.

TSMC is expanding capacity but slowly: its new Tainan fab begins volume production in the first half of 2027 and Musk's Arizona fab follows in the second half. Samsung’s Taylor, Texas facility targets AI5 on 2nm with volume production also expected by the second half of 2027.

Tesla delivered roughly 1.6 million vehicles last year, each needing a self-driving computer, while Optimus ramp is measured in thousands even under an aggressive plan that puts AI5 into robots around April 2027 and pushes external deliveries to late 2027. Electrek argues both Musk's 'AI4 is enough' framing and the supply constraint can be true simultaneously, but only one explains the timing—pointing to Tesla’s memory cuts as evidence of rationing rather than choice.
items.title: Tesla's scarce AI5 chips are heading to Optimus first, not cars

The Bird Protection and Study Society of Serbia (BPSSS) is opposing a nearly 500-hectare photovoltaic plant and battery energy storage system planned for the municipality of Opovo, arguing that it threatens rare salt marsh habitats. The special purpose vehicle Baranda Energetski Park intends to build a solar power plant alongside a battery energy storage system spanning about 493 hectares on former salt marsh lakes and fishponds.

BPSSS submitted formal objections demanding rejection of the draft detailed regulation plan, which was open for public comment until October 21. The society criticized that documents were only available at the municipal building rather than online, reducing public scrutiny, and argued the project serves private investor interests over local community benefit by rezoning fishponds away from fish farming, sport fishing, and ecotourism.

Marko Šćiban, an ornithologist at BPSSS, said the society supports renewable energy but insists it must use environmentally acceptable sites. He described this case as the opposite of that principle, noting the project would backfill inland saline ponds representing rare, endangered habitats important for biodiversity conservation.

BPSSS data records 185 bird species and over 102 algae species in the wider area, with Center for Biodiversity Information figures showing 127 species of conservation significance present, including 18 designated as relict, endemic, or rare. The society also proposed installing solar panels on houses and buildings to achieve comparable electricity output at lower cost.

The plan is a second draft following the first adopted in 2025; capacity was increased from 300 MW to 317 MW and a battery added requiring new planning documentation, with revised documents referring to multiple units for phased construction.
items.title: Serbia's bird protection society opposes Opovo solar project

According to a Bloomberg report, restricted Nvidia Corp. Blackwell artificial intelligence processors have appeared inside a large-scale data centre in Shanghai connected to Alice Huang, the Singapore-based founder of a cloud company that Washington blacklisted earlier this month. The finding is based on regulatory documents submitted to Chinese authorities in November 2026.

Those documents indicate that two Chinese companies installed Nvidia's flagship Blackwell-powered systems at the Yangtze River Delta Project in Shanghai. Among the equipment reportedly placed there are a GB300 NVL72 rack and a GB200 server.
items.title: Restricted Nvidia Chips Found at Shanghai Data Centre Linked to Blacklisted Megaspeed

On Friday, Chile's competition authority (FNE) asked the country's antitrust court to fine Apple about $80 million and order corrective measures for abusing its dominant position in the iOS operating system market. The regulator said the US technology firm has restricted competition in app distribution and in-app payments for digital goods on iOS since at least 2019.

The FNE stated that the sought fine is equivalent to 30 per cent of sales from the product lines and services linked to the infringement during the period investigated. The regulator said it verified that Apple has prevented sideloading of applications and alternative app stores from web browsers on iPhone devices, forcing developers and consumers to rely exclusively on the App Store. Apple argued the restrictions were necessary for security and privacy reasons, but the FNE found those measures unnecessary and disproportionate.

The FNE wants the antitrust court to require Apple to allow third-party apps and app stores, alternative in-app billing, and payment buttons that send users to external payment systems without friction.
items.title: Chile's antitrust authority seeks $80 million Apple fine over iOS

items.summary:
OpenAI is set to introduce a significant change to its paid subscription plans, effective in December. Under the new system, users on the ChatGPT Plus, Pro, and Business tiers will have a single shared usage limit covering both ChatGPT and Codex instead of separate limits for each service. OpenAI states that this step aligns with incorporating ChatGPT's agentic capabilities into its core experience.

The change directly affects users who regularly use Codex alongside ChatGPT, though the company has clarified that Instant Chat will be excluded from this shared limit. Usage across both services will now be measured on a token basis rather than separately tracked by service or task type. OpenAI notes that consumption varies depending on which model is used and what kind of work is performed, with advanced models and more complex tasks generally consuming more tokens.

OpenAI plans to give users visibility into their remaining usage limit and reset timing through the Usage section in ChatGPT's Settings menu, where combined information for both services will be displayed. If a user exhausts their shared limit, they have three options: wait for the limit to reset, upgrade their subscription plan, or purchase credits to continue using features covered under this arrangement.

Before rolling out the change broadly, OpenAI is testing it on a limited scale so that some users may see the new usage system before December. The company says feedback from these testers will help assess potential issues and ensure minimal disruption to existing workflows during the transition.
items.title: OpenAI to Share ChatGPT and Codex Limits for Paid Users from December

VoxDev's episode dated November 27, 2026 featured research spanning migration, HIV testing, tuition waivers, and growth philanthropy. The graduation programmes segment highlighted that while strong results from NGO-led pilots have encouraged governments in around 75 countries to adopt the approach (ev1), experimental gains often shrink or vanish when scaled up; new evidence comes from Bihar, where the state government expanded the model to 155,000 ultra-poor households. Abhijit Banerjee discussed this expansion on VoxDevTalks, and Ellie Horrocks joined Ideas in Development to discuss growth philanthropy, including how success is measured, attribution of impact, and where new funding should go.

A separate episode examined historical migration: following the Confederate defeat in the US Civil War, between 5,000 and 10,000 US Southerners (the Confederados) migrated to Brazil, many settling in São Paulo. João Tampellini discussed how these skilled migrants brought agricultural knowledge, business experience, and capital that were relatively scarce in the region, helping turn a poor area into an industrial hub, though only cultural traits anchored in their churches and schools outlasted them.

In public health research across sub-Saharan Africa, women from ancestrally matrilineal ethnic groups are much more likely to be HIV-positive than those from patrilineal groups (Jordan Loper), largely because less stable marriages lead to more partner changes and less condom use; making routine, low-stigma HIV testing widely available can help. In Tamil Nadu, Gopinath Annadurai and Soham Sahoo evaluated the First-Generation Graduate Scholarship, a large-scale affirmative-action programme providing tuition waivers to first-generation students, finding it raises technical degree completion and improves early labour-market outcomes.

Elsewhere in development coverage included Charles Kenny on lessons from the Nepal dam disaster, Max Roser on loneliness in poorer countries, and open calls for papers for the 20th International Conference on Migration and Development with a February 1st deadline (ev5).
items.title: This Week in Development Economics at VoxDev

items.summary:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei dismissed reports that his company is surrendering human control of decisions to superintelligent AI as 'absurd,' according to Axios. He argued that governance by legitimate democratic processes should never be sacrificed for efficiency or security, and said the case against autocracy applies equally to AI-driven governance.

An Anthropic spokesperson told Axios that Claude is trained not to undermine human oversight, even though some employees believe humanity ought to cede part of its authority over decisions to superintelligent systems. Amodei distinguished between surrendering free will in a broad sense and letting AI handle specific tasks with less human involvement—such as driving cars or writing software end-to-end—and said his view on task automation is mixed, noting it can save lives but also carries downsides.

Amodei flagged recursive self-improvement, where AI builds successive generations of models without meaningful human supervision, stating that Anthropic does not expect Claude to build frontier models fully autonomously. He added that pausing or scaling back some deployments could be warranted so people have time to adjust to job disruption, and said he is willing to risk the company's future by refusing to let its models be used for autonomous weapons—a stance no other AI company has taken.

He claimed other AI companies hold similar views on automating specific tasks but criticized some CEOs for repeating slogans like 'human control and agency' without changing their products. Rival leaders weighed in, with Meta Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang writing that society should not accept a handover to AI, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman saying he wants people to retain agency over the future.

Amodei's concerns follow an essay from September urging AI companies to pull back on their most advanced model development. Separately, Anthropic reported in June that Claude wrote over 80% of the code added to its own codebase.
items.title: Anthropic CEO Rejects Reports That Company Surrendered Human Control to AI

items.summary:
Nvidia has instructed manufacturing partners including Dell and Super Micro Computer to pause server deliveries bound for Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia. The directive comes as Nvidia examines its regional partners more closely to comply with American export rules, and there is a mechanism under which held shipments can be cleared later. According to The Wall Street Journal, the instruction was relayed to Dell and Super Micro without an announced duration.

The move follows Washington's effort to prevent Nvidia's advanced processors from reaching Chinese firms, since part of China's computing power has come through remotely accessed data centers located in those four countries. The Wall Street Journal cited the think tank Institute for Progress for reporting that such remotely accessed data centers have accounted for about 24% of the computing capacity China uses for artificial intelligence.

The Commerce Department issued an interim final rule earlier this month requiring data center operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil to obtain U.S. licenses before buying advanced AI processors from Nvidia and other American companies. The Bureau of Industry and Security said the rule aims to stop companies from circumventing limits on sensitive technology by tapping chips remotely through foreign data centers, with licenses issued case by case.

Malaysia's Trade Minister Johari Abdul Ghani said Kuala Lumpur does not intend to negotiate with Washington over the rule and expects operators to comply. Singapore said it is studying the measure, while China's Foreign Ministry called the rules 'economic coercion.' The pause could affect cloud-computing providers and American companies relying on Nvidia chips hosted in those countries; firms seeking project funding may face lenders hesitant to commit capital until the pause ends.

Firmus Grid, a cloud provider that counts Nvidia among its backers, disclosed in September that it is constructing two Malaysian data centers for OpenAI. The company is also developing facilities in Indonesia and Singapore.
items.title: Nvidia Pauses AI Server Shipments to Four Southeast Asian Countries

items.summary:
Proposed new US tariffs have triggered a backlash among allies and rivals, raising fears of renewed trade tensions with China ahead of another leaders' summit in two weeks. Many US trading partners are already frustrated over alleged Chinese overcapacity, which they say is driving surging exports that hollow out their domestic industries; Bloomberg noted that hitting those countries with levies could undermine Washington's push to move supply chains away from China by making alternative locations less attractive.

The tariffs target multiple countries' alleged overproduction and risk turning governments that share American concerns about China against the US. One analyst argued that accusing India of having 'excess industrial capacity' is not only delusional but so detached from reality it could occur in an alternate one.
items.title: Backlash Grows Over Proposed US Tariffs

items.summary:
Chris O'Shea, chief executive of Centrica and the owner of British Gas, told staff at its largest gas storage facility that he was seeking urgent talks with Andy Burnham to save jobs. The company reportedly said it would do everything possible to preserve employment while pursuing discussions with trade unions, Whitehall officials, and the prime minister.

The message came after the government rebuffed Centrica's plea for short-term support to run the Rough facility over winter and delayed its response to a longer-term consultation on ageing underground gas stores. The Guardian reported that the government delivered its decision in recent weeks, with O'Shea using an internal memo seen by Sky News to update staff about continuing talks.

The Rough site supports roughly 400 jobs across direct employees and contractors but is scheduled to close at the end of March unless the government intervenes, as it has become uneconomic to operate. Facilities normally store gas in summer when prices are lower and sell it in winter during higher demand, but successive energy crises have disrupted this pattern and made investment in needed upgrades difficult.

The warning follows similar concerns from Centrica about the site's future and comes less than two weeks after SSE told investors it would shut its Atwick storage facility next summer without government support. Neso used a second consecutive annual report to warn that the UK faces gas supply crisis risk as North Sea production declines, noting that even an unlikely outage during a cold spell could leave Britain short of gas.

Centrica is listed on the FTSE 100 with a value of nearly £7bn, and a company spokesperson declined to comment.
items.title: Centrica Boss Seeks Urgent Government Talks Over Rough Gas Storage Facility

items.summary:
Norse Atlantic Airways has filed for bankruptcy and cancelled all future flights, its chief executive Eivind Roald announced in a statement to the Oslo stock exchange. The board concluded that operations were no longer viable after surging fuel costs caused by the Iran war destroyed its finances over the past year. Norse posted a message on its website advising customers not to come to airports and telling those stranded away from home to contact their travel agents, flight bookers, insurers or credit card companies, while making clear customer service was no longer available by phone, email, chat or social media.

The collapse followed a day in which the airline put flights on hold with a warning that its finances were critical. Norse operated low-cost long-haul routes from London Gatwick and Manchester to Thailand, South Africa and the US among other destinations, all of which have now been scrapped along with ticket sales being halted across UK operations. The board said airlines worldwide had suffered spiralling oil prices that doubled jet fuel costs while dampening consumer demand after the Iran war began in February.

Rival airlines predicted surging fares and the collapse of weaker carriers as a result. Norse was founded in 2021 attempting to emulate Norwegian Air's low-cost long-haul model, briefly reviving transatlantic routes with Boeing 787 Dreamliners before hitting similar financial trouble this summer when it explored a sale or merger.

The company had embarked on a $50m (£38m) cost-cutting programme that included shedding jobs and its Norwegian headquarters. On Friday morning, aircraft lessors served termination notices for the 12 planes in Norse's fleet as part of the abrupt end to operations.
items.title: Norse Atlantic Airways Files for Bankruptcy and Cancels All Flights

The US Federal Communications Commission authorized Elon Musk's SpaceX on Wednesday to deploy one million satellites under its Starmind constellation, a fleet that would dwarf the total number of active satellites currently in orbit and support space-based data centres for AI computing. The approval follows Starlink as part of an expanding megaconstellation trend involving Amazon and Chinese operators, but it raises new concerns about space debris, atmospheric pollution, and changes to the night sky.

University College London researchers estimated that one million satellites could increase emissions from launches and re-entries by roughly 70 to 150 times current levels, potentially affecting ozone, climate, and air quality. The FCC said those emission questions fell outside its remit and dismissed concerns about atmospheric pollution from burning-up satellites as speculative and unsupported in the record.

European Space Agency data showed more than 231 million debris objects between one millimetre and ten centimetres were already orbiting Earth as of February 1. University of Birmingham professor Hugh Lewis warned that even a one per cent failure rate could leave thousands of derelict satellites each year, increasing collision risk.

The American Astronomical Society said the constellation would undermine astronomical facilities, with sun-synchronous satellites potentially contaminating images and visible bands outnumbering stars in simulations shared by Virginia Tech's Shane Ross. The FCC rejected additional conditions on optical astronomy protection but accepted SpaceX's commitment to coordinate with the National Science Foundation.

SpaceX told regulators it would initially deploy at lower altitudes for testing before moving higher, using onboard propulsion for collision avoidance, station-keeping, and controlled re-entries over oceans where satellites are designed to burn up completely. The FCC requires a first satellite by November 2033, half the fleet by 2038, and completion by 2040.

SpaceX's largest single rocket carries only 143 payloads, making simultaneous launch of one million impossible; operators sometimes request higher numbers for design flexibility. SpaceX sought approval for 42,000 Starlink satellites before deploying a system that now has just over 11,000 in space, and no operator has ever sent one million objects into orbit.

The network is central to Musk's vision of moving energy-intensive AI computing into orbit with solar-powered data centres. However, SpaceX told investors ahead of its stock market listing that the ambition relied on unproven technology and may not be commercially viable.
items.title: FCC Approves SpaceX's Starmind Constellation of One Million Satellites

items.summary: In Mexico, a growing wave of Amazon delivery problems has drawn public attention after two customers posted their experiences on X. Zaira Hernández ordered an iPhone but received perfume, while Itzel Ayari bought a Nintendo Switch 2 and found a fly killer lamp instead; both shared cases that accumulated thousands of responses. The pattern behind these incidents involves high-value electronics arriving in sealed Amazon packages containing different items of similar weight, such as perfumes, portable batteries, soap bars, or cartons of milk. This raises concerns about a security failure across the distribution chain at what is described as the world's largest e-commerce company, alongside difficulties for buyers seeking refunds. Zaira Hernández reported that her first call to Amazon customer service requested proof, and on subsequent contact she was told no refund would be possible because the safety bag appeared unaffected. She said even recording when she opened the package did not get them to take responsibility, despite repeated email attempts. In its response to EL PAÍS, Amazon expressed regret over affected customers' experiences while stating it has reviewed cases and taken necessary actions. Patricia Luna received a portable battery instead of an iPhone in November 2025 and documented her lengthy refund struggle through the mobile app before turning to Concilianet, Profeco's virtual dispute-resolution site. After months of process requiring documents such as ID and payment receipts, she presented her case at a hearing held five months after purchase; both the federal agency and company ruled in her favor. Luna was refunded almost half a year later, around mid-May, and advised others to keep evidence throughout since complaints are accepted through Profeco even though the process is slow. She noted that these are not products costing 100 pesos, urging people not to give up.
items.title: Amazon Delivery Mix-ups Spark Frustration Among Mexican Online Shoppers

items.summary:
Anthony Moretti of Robert Morris University argues in a CGTN opinion piece that the Trump administration's tariff policy damages both American citizens and international trade cooperation. The proposed Washington plan, set to take effect next year, would raise tariffs by as much as 20% on imports from China, the European Union and other trading partners, with some Chinese goods taxed at 40% or higher (ev2, ev3). Moretti contends that White House justifications based on an investigation into excess manufacturing capacity represent a flawed excuse for labeling foreign production.

The author focuses largely on how tariffs have already hurt Americans, citing US News reporting that clothing costs rose 7.5%, motor vehicles and parts by 4.7%, and household furnishings by 3.2% (ev4, ev5, ev6). One estimate projects the typical American family will spend about $2500 in 2026 on tariffs, roughly under $50 per week (ev7, dt8, ev9), while all of US News's cited food categories face double-digit increases. Moretti also attributes recent midterm losses to voters across both chambers and multiple governor mansions as a rebuke to the president over economic policy.

The piece adds that tariffs strain small businesses, with the US Chamber of Commerce estimating increased costs exceeding $200 billion (ev10) and the Center for American Progress projecting an extra $24,000 per month in import payments between March 2025 and August 2026 (dt11, dt12, ev13). Moretti concludes that tariffs undermine multilateral rules to serve 'America First' ideology, would trigger reciprocal responses from affected nations raising their prices too, and contradict commitments made by US and Chinese leaders for constructive stability in China-US relations.
items.title: US tariffs policy harms global trade cooperation

items.summary:
Pablo Hernández de Cos is set to succeed Christine Lagarde as president of the European Central Bank, which sets interest rates for the 359 million people in the eurozone (ev1). The choice comes amid high inflation driven by the Iran war and concerns over government debt across Europe. Leaders from the 21 EU countries that use the euro backed Hernández de Cos along with candidates for two other top posts at the ECB (ev2).

Hernández de Cos currently leads the Bank for International Settlements in Basel, Switzerland, and served on the ECB's rate-setting Governing Council from 2018 to 2024 as head of Spain's central bank (dt3). Analysts expect him to bring his consensus-building reputation while taking a more active role than Lagarde in shaping monetary policy. Andrew Kenningham, chief Europe economist at Capital Economics, described him as 'an economists' economist,' technically highly competent and respected, though he would be more likely to challenge advice from the Chief Economist than his predecessor.

Kenningham sees Hernández de Cos leaning toward lower rates, consistent with a forecast that the ECB may raise rates by just another quarter of a percentage point before starting cuts by end of 2027 (dt5). Eurozone inflation was 4% in October, above the bank's 2% target (ev6, ev7), and the ECB could still raise rates on 17 December when Lagarde chairs the meeting. ING's Carsten Brezski expects Hernández de Cos to leave a clearer personal mark on policy than his predecessor, while Commerzbank analysts' review of his speeches suggests he is among the monetary policy doves who lean toward lower rates.

In 2020, Hernández de Cos backed the ECB's pandemic bond-buying programme, which was expanded to €1.85 trillion (dt8, ev9). Commerzbank analyst Marco Wagner noted that rising government debt may make governments prefer a dovish president, with France struggling under high debt and rising interest costs.

Hernández de Cos won out over former Dutch central bank head Klaas Knot, who was regarded as a hawk favoring higher rates. The European Council also put forward France's Laurence Boone and Germany's Markus Brunnermeier for two seats on the ECB's six-member executive board. Brezski suggested France played a key role in shifting support from Knot to De Cos and may have prioritized securing the role held by Isabel Schnabel, who oversees market operations.

Kenningham sees Boone as more likely to favor lower rates than Schnabel she would replace, while Brunnermeier is seen as more likely to favor higher rates than Philip Lane. The net impact on policy will probably be small, though their positions remain to be seen once in post. The European Parliament and the ECB's Governing Council will be consulted before EU leaders make formal appointments.

Lagarde, 70, announced she would step down on 7 February 2027 (dt10), around nine months before the end of her eight-year term, so she could speak more freely about issues beyond monetary policy. She said in July that she was not a candidate for anything and played down speculation about running in France's presidential election. In November, Lagarde said a leadership role at the World Economic Forum was one of her options after leaving the ECB.

Lagarde is regarded as pragmatic, building consensus among national central bank governors while resisting being labeled a hawk or dove; she called herself an 'owl,' associated with wisdom in Greek and Roman mythology. She congratulated Hernández de Cos on Thursday, praising his intellect, warmth, and good humor.
items.title: ECB leadership transition and its implications for eurozone interest rates

items.summary:
Indonesia's Coordinating Minister for Economic Affairs Airlangga Hartarto told Euronews in an exclusive interview that US tariffs pushed the EU and Indonesia closer as they finalized a trade deal signed in Brussels after about a decade of talks. He said he expects the agreement to lift bilateral trade by 50% within three years, noting the target was discussed with both European partners and business groups from each side. Hartarto described Jakarta and Europe's economies as compatible rather than competing because their products differ.

The minister also addressed investor concerns after MSCI proposed downgrading Indonesia from 'emerging' to 'standalone' status by end of June 2027, which would remove Indonesian shares from its emerging markets indices. He likened the warning to a broken window and said the economy is in better shape than suggested, citing growth of 5.45% in the first nine months of 2026.

Hartarto projected that next week's New Asia Forum investment conference could yield deals worth up to $30 billion (€27.4bn) regionally, with Danantara expecting about 40% to 50% going to Indonesia. He also referenced OECD reports supporting Indonesia's semiconductor ambitions and its goal of joining the group by 2028.

On compliance deadlines, Hartarto said Indonesian exporters face EU deforestation rules from 30 December requiring proof goods were not produced on land deforested after 2020, though his government has asked for national certification to count. He also noted Indonesia leaves the EU's Generalised Scheme of Preferences on 1 January, but expressed confidence the trade deal would be implemented provisionally in early 2027.

The European Council reported last year's EU-Indonesia goods trade was worth €28.9 billion, and Jakarta's IDX Composite benchmark index had fallen roughly 38% this year according to Hartarto.
items.title: Indonesia's Economy Minister Airlangga Hartarto Speaks on Trade and Investment

items.summary:
Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali has begun his journey to the China Space Station, marking a new chapter in cooperation between Pakistan and China. The item notes that an earlier mission offers researchers on the ground a preview of what such collaboration can produce: seven seeds of Pakistani medicinal plants traveled to the station aboard Shenzhou-14 in 2022 and returned to Pakistan in February 2023.

More than three years after their handover, research on those seeds continues. Liu Xinmin, a professor at Ningbo University who helped organize the Chinese side of the seed project, told CGTN that as of now more than 30 Chinese and Pakistani institutions are involved in the wider cooperation, including government agencies, universities, and research institutes. He said the work has also laid groundwork for training researchers, building joint laboratories, and developing health products.

A Zhejiang-Pakistan joint laboratory for traditional medicine was unveiled in June 2026, with Pakistani partners including the International Center for Chemical and Biological Sciences at the University of Karachi and the University of Lahore. Liu described the ties as personal, saying he and his Pakistani partners call one another 'brothers' when they meet, a word he said they mean sincerely rather than merely as courtesy.

He hopes younger researchers will carry that relationship forward, pointing to Dr. Inam Ullah, a Pakistani fellow at Ningbo University's Institute of Drug Discovery Technology. Inam told CGTN that watching the seeds travel from Pakistan made him more certain about continuing his research in China, and he cited the country's research opportunities, advanced technologies, well-equipped labs, and professors as factors behind his decision.

Driss El Hadani, deputy director of the United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs during an interview in September, said a space mission's influence can extend beyond those who travel into orbit. He noted that institutions, universities, and industries contribute to such missions, and their participation could create 'a new dynamic' helping countries develop space activities.
items.title: Pakistani Astronaut Begins China Space Station Mission Amid Growing Scientific Ties

items.summary: A group of foreign scholars traveled across several innovation hubs in Beijing to observe modernization firsthand, exploring the Zhongguancun National Innovation Demonstration Zone Exhibition Center, Digital and Intelligent Haidian Innovation Exhibition Center, and AI Origin Community. During their visit they examined smart city systems and new artificial intelligence tools up close. The trip was framed around the question of how countries can learn from one another while pursuing modernization in ways suited to themselves. The scholars shared key takeaways about what they observed during the field trip.
items.title: Foreign Scholars Visit Beijing's Innovation Sites on China Modernization Trip

items.summary:
Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden described a disruption to the Department for Work and Pensions as a 'serious cyber incident,' saying some services were taken offline on precautionary grounds after unusual activity was detected, with no evidence yet that any personal details had been compromised. Regular benefits and pensions payments would continue as normal according to the department, though members of the public reported not receiving expected payments on Friday morning while trying to check state pension or claim universal credit.

The cause remains unconfirmed; No 10 declined to rule out a hack but said there was no evidence that other government departments were being targeted. Debbie Abrahams, chair of the work and pensions committee, backed the department's swift action to contain the incident while noting it is critical to investigate the impact on service users.

Cyber security expert Luis Costa from Surfshark warned scammers could exploit the disruption by posing as DWP representatives to claimants worried about missed payments. Separately, Kemi Badenoch confirmed that all Conservative candidates must sign a 'candidate covenant' committing them to leaving the European Convention on Human Rights and dropping the net zero target for 2050. Around one in three of England's roughly 9,369 rough sleepers had been offered a route off the streets under Andy Burnham's Christmas pledge, while nearly 100 Labour MPs urged Burnham to reject drilling at the Rosebank oilfield.
items.title: UK pensions department hit by serious cyber incident
