items.summary: A segment of the Path to Zero series explores whether used cooking oil from restaurant kitchens can serve as a fuel for commercial aircraft. The piece notes that while electric vehicles are growing in use on roads, powering commercial planes without fossil fuels remains a significant challenge. It suggests part of the solution may come from an everyday waste product: the spent cooking oil left behind after food preparation.
items.title: Used Cooking Oil Could Power Sustainable Flights

items.summary:
Scientists are studying how much carbon the desert forests of northwest China can store and what role protection plays, according to a Path to Zero episode. The research focuses on Ganjiahu National Nature Reserve in Xinjiang, which contains Asia's largest white saxaul forest.

The crew traveled into the desert to meet researchers uncovering these hidden carbon stores and exploring their significance for China's path toward carbon neutrality.
items.title: China Researchers Investigate Carbon Storage in Xinjiang Desert Forests

items.summary:
Spain's prime minister Pedro Sánchez said on Friday that he was convinced his Socialist party would win a snap general election, insisting internal data suggested victory even as nearly all pre-ban polls favored a conservative People's Party–Vox coalition. He told radio station SER 'I can't conceive of us losing,' arguing left-leaning voters were mobilizing to secure a progressive majority needed to address the country's housing crisis.

The election is set for 29 November, and most released polling showed Vox poised to pick up almost 20% of the vote. Sánchez called the snap election on 5 October after PP, Vox, and Catalan party Junts voted down emergency measures addressing the housing crisis that had triggered large protests across Spain.

A legal ban prohibits publishing new opinion surveys in the five days before an election, prompting a company owned by Prensa Ibérica to run 'The Adelaide Review' poll during the blackout period. Closing rallies were scheduled for Madrid and Seville/Valencia on campaign day, with voters observing a reflection day before Sunday's vote.
items.title: Spanish PM Sánchez confident despite adverse polls

items.summary:
A court in Mombasa, Kenya, has found Paul Mackenzie guilty of the manslaughter of 123 followers of his Christian doomsday cult. The conviction relates to ordering all adult members to fast until death in Shakahola forest near the coast between January 2021 and September 2023.

Mackenzie had earlier this month been jailed for 200 years for murdering 191 people, mostly children, in a separate mass killing. The court also convicted 29 others, including his wife Rhoda Mumbua Maweu, of their part in the manslaughter, while 60 defendants were acquitted and the Director of Public Prosecutions indicated an appeal would be launched against those acquittals.

Prosecutors argued Mackenzie acted with accomplices as part of a suicide pact to fast to death 'to meet Jesus', with children meant to die first followed by women and then men, while witnesses testified he preached that education, medicine and ornaments were sinful. The defendants claimed the victims had fasted out of their own free will.

The verdict was described by Kenya's Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions as 'the final conviction' in the Shakahola cases against Mackenzie. His arrest followed the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves, and the case prompted President William Ruto to set up a commission of inquiry into oversight of rogue religious activity, though that was later declared unconstitutional.
items.title: Kenyan doomsday cult leader convicted over further 123 deaths

items.summary:
Brazil has expressed regret over a statement by French President Emmanuel Macron, who described Brazilian meat as 'doped' while meeting farming union representatives at the Élysée Palace. The comment came during his celebration of EU restrictions on imports of Brazilian meat and poultry that took effect in September, part of an ongoing trade dispute between the EU and Mercosur over antimicrobial use in animal production.

Brazil's government said Macron's remarks 'spread misinformation' and contradicted available scientific evidence about its animal protein sector. The country defended itself by citing decades of supplying animal protein to the EU, exports to 177 markets, a rigorous sanitary control system corroborated by a recent European audit, and compliance with stringent environmental requirements. Brazil also characterized the restrictions as politically motivated and urged France to reconsider in light of scientific evidence while affirming that its bilateral relationship should be guided by mutual respect.

Brazil highlighted that it is a major meat exporter, noting some $1.84bn (£1.4bn) worth of beef went to EU markets alone in 2025, according to Brazil's agricultural ministry.
items.title: Brazil Pushes Back on Macron Calling Its Meat 'Doped'

items.summary:
Tottenham Hotspur forward Savio is set to miss the busy Christmas Premier League fixtures after suffering a recurrence of a hamstring injury, manager Roberto De Zerbi said on Friday. The Brazilian made his first matchday squad appearance in six weeks during Tottenham's 2-0 home win over Ipswich Town last weekend, coming off the bench in the 64th minute before being forced off with two minutes remaining.

De Zerbi confirmed at a pre-match press conference ahead of Sunday's visit to Sunderland that this was a recurrence of the same hamstring problem and ruled Savio out for the festive period. Describing it as 'a tough situation to accept,' he noted that while the 22-year-old is suffering from these new injuries, they are part of football.

The manager declined to give an exact recovery timeline but suggested it could take between 50 and 80 days, adding that Savio will be crucial for Tottenham's final stretch of the season.
items.title: Spurs' Savio Ruled Out Over Christmas With Recurring Hamstring Injury

items.summary:
Dutch authorities seized more than two dozen critically endangered Vallarta mud turtles from the luggage of a man flying to Hong Kong via Amsterdam's Schiphol Airport. The Netherlands Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA) announced the seizure on Friday, saying customs officers discovered the animals during a routine inspection on November 21 before alerting the agency about live fauna.

The NVWA reported that police arrested the man at its request and he remained in custody while federal prosecutors continued their investigation. Most of the turtles were packed in a box beside a toy car, with others sealed inside a sock within a suitcase; they had been wrapped in duct tape to prevent movement but all survived the journey.

The Vallarta mud turtles are endemic to western Mexico's Jalisco state and only entered the taxonomical record in 2018. The NVWA estimated that about 300 of these animals remain in the wild, noting that suspected poaching of 26 may have reduced the population by nearly 10%. The Turtle Island organization in Graz, Austria considers them 'the world's smallest turtle species' and estimates over 99% of their natural habitat has been lost to urbanization. These freshwater turtles are known to grow no larger than 10 centimeters (less than 4 inches) in length.

The IUCN Red List classifies the Vallarta mud turtle as 'Critically Endangered,' and it is subject to the highest level of protection under CITES. The NVWA urged people to report suspected illegal trade of protected species through online forums, marketplaces, bird fairs, or antique and curiosity markets.
items.title: Netherlands Seizes Critically Endangered Turtles From Passenger Luggage

items.summary:
“Refugee families use agroforestry to restore degraded landscape in Bangladesh camp”

After the 2017 influx of Rohingya people, more than 1,500 hectares of protected forest were cleared across Cox's Bazar to build shelters and provide firewood. The Bangladeshi government had allocated roughly 2,500 hectares (6,100 acres) of that land for the settlements. Stripping away vegetation left hillsides bare and sandy, turning seasonal rain into a recurring crisis of landslides and soil erosion.

Rohingya families are now using traditional agroecology techniques on agroforestry plots to heal the degraded landscape while growing food amid cuts to international aid. Supported by NGOs such as UNHCR and FAO, large-scale reforestation projects have planted nearly one million tree seedlings and restored 200 hectares of camp land with a mix of fast-growing species and deep-rooted native trees, including fruit trees, to stabilize the slopes.

The techniques combine multi-layered intercropping, organic composting from household waste and animal manure, and seed saving. Across the camps, more than 159,000 refugees are engaged in homestead gardening, though not all use agroecology methods; some rely on chemical sprays and paddy fields instead.

FAO reports that these efforts have restored degraded forest land and improved ecosystem services, while a dry-season planting pilot achieved a 100% seedling survival rate at trial sites. UNHCR SuLMER staff say the programs integrate Rohingya knowledge of planting, fertilizer use, pest control, harvesting timing, and space-maximizing designs like sack and vertical gardening.

The long-term survival of restored areas is threatened by funding shortages and a lack of secure land rights for refugees under Bangladeshi law. The Government of Bangladesh has stated that the Rohingya are there temporarily and expected to repatriate when conditions allow, leaving the future care of reforested slopes uncertain.
items.title: Rohingya refugees restore degraded Bangladesh camp land with agroforestry

visual.alt: Bar chart. Forest area cleared 1,500 hectare; Camp land restored by agencies 200 hectare.

items.summary:
Nearly 120 residents of Vindoulou, a neighborhood in Pointe-Noire, Republic of Congo, filed a civil claim before the city's High Court in October 2026 seeking compensation and medical care for suspected lead exposure linked to the nearby Metssa Congo battery recycling plant. The facility opened in 2013 as part of the UAE-based Metssa Group and recycled car batteries into exportable lead bars until it closed in 2024, though residents say no cleanup has occurred since.

Blood tests conducted by residents with Amnesty International support in 2023 found blood lead levels far above the WHO's recommended threshold of 5 micrograms per deciliter, with some readings up to 10 times higher. In May 2026, Columbia University researcher Alexander Van Geen worked with the community to collect and analyze 49 soil samples extending about 300 meters from the former plant; nearly half exceeded the EPA's residential safety threshold of 200 milligrams per kilogram, seven by more than tenfold, with a peak near 10,000 mg/kg. Van Geen mapped contamination as severe close to the site but decreasing rapidly with distance.

The analysis concluded that about 25,000 square meters outside the plant were affected and could be remediated through removing roughly the top 10 centimeters of soil at a cost lower than decontaminating the plant itself. Residents' collective president Cyrille Traoré Ndembi said authorities have not responded to requests for information or action since operations halted, while experts including Jacques Gardon of France's IRD called the findings clear proof of pollution and urged further blood testing.

Van Geen plans a follow-up survey of about 300 samples near an adjacent school this fall using low-cost community-based soil kits developed in a 2025 study by Samantha Moura, Daphne van der Molen, and himself. The plant's representatives have not responded to requests for comment.
items.title: Vindoulou Residents Sue Over Lead Pollution From Metssa Congo Foundry

items.summary:
North Korea has modified its national flag as part of a constitutional amendment that enshrined the country's status as a nuclear power and removed any reference to the 'peaceful reunification' pursued by Kim Jong Un's predecessors. The changes accompany an effort by the reclusive leader to demonstrate his desire to expand diplomatic ties with friendly nations, according to Yuka Royer speaking with Edward Howell of Oxford University.

The broadcast also covered several other developments. China has placed Shanghai's Communist Party chief under investigation for 'suspected violations of discipline and laws,' a euphemism commonly used for corruption; Chen Jining is described as a rising figure who was once seen as a possible contender for the country's highest governing body, making him the fourth senior Communist Party leader purged from President Xi Jinping's top team since last year. Additionally, Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali became the first person from his country to orbit the Earth and the first foreign national to stay aboard China's Tiangong space station.

The landmark mission is framed as highlighting Beijing's ambition to rival the US by turning its space station into an international research hub.
items.title: North Korea Amends Constitution Under New Flag, Enshrines Nuclear Status

items.summary:
Norwegian low-cost long-haul airline Norse Atlantic's operating unit declared bankruptcy on Friday, following a Wednesday warning that its financial situation was critical and the suspension of all flights while it sought emergency funding. The carrier attributed its distress largely to sharply higher jet fuel prices in 2026 driven by the war in Iran and resulting Middle East tensions.

Norse reported that its lessors had terminated leasing contracts for all 12 aircraft in its fleet, demanding their return; the company initially planned to contest this before announcing plans to file. CEO Eivind Roald said the board made the difficult decision despite extensive efforts to find a solution, while noting that the listed parent Norse Atlantic ASA and the UK subsidiary remain outside the filing as they seek to continue operations.

The carrier had warned on Thursday it would file for bankruptcy unless financing could be arranged, stating there can be no assurance of a viable outcome. Founded five years ago in Arendal, Norway, with 12 planes serving 14 destinations, Norse Atlantic recorded a net loss of $61.9 million (€56.5 million) in 2025 before the war's added strains.

The conflict has hit small and low-cost airlines hardest as global fuel deliveries face severe disruption from reduced traffic through the Strait of Hormuz after US attacks on Iran in early 2026, which pushed aviation fuel to more than double its price at peak. Prices rose higher than during Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and climbed again after a mid-summer dip as hopes for resolution faded into stalemate, marking the worst crisis since COVID cut air traffic from 2020 onward.
items.title: Norse Atlantic Files for Bankruptcy Amid Jet Fuel Costs

items.summary:
“When an American influencer recommends a bar in Spain: why Spaniards are fascinated by how foreigners see them” is EL PAÍS USA Edition's exploration of how foreign content creators on social media influence the way Spanish cities and culture are perceived. Katie Boggs, a 26-year-old American creator based in Barcelona for four years, says her videos have changed since she arrived with expectations shaped by cheap living; she now avoids recommending cafés or moving to Spain because of mass tourism's artificial, low-quality vibe that crowds out genuine cultural connection. Thousands of Instagram and TikTok accounts document foreigners' lives in Spain, mixing humor, cultural outreach, and promotion of 'authentic' spots that hospitality companies may pay for.

The piece traces this dynamic back to the early 19th century, when French travelogues by Alexandre Dumas, Théophile Gautier, and George Sand popularized clichés about Spain's laidback character — now echoed in British and German recommendations of 'the best Mallorcan spots.' Anthropologist Amarna Miller argues the tourist/traveler distinction is an elitist fiction since everyone uses tourism infrastructure, while creator Maggie Dickmann rejects the expat label as classism. Professor Paula Simó from the University of Valencia warns that high-income newcomers can be regressive when housing supply is rigid and regulation weak, stressing that the debate should focus on income rather than passport.

Simó contends internet-optimized communication flattens cultural complexity into visual codes and turns residents into backdrops, with content now emphasizing lifestyle themes like siesta, partying, midnight dinners, street life, and low cost of living rooted in economic asymmetry. Journalist Kyle Chayka's FilterWorld analysis is cited for describing how popular destinations become subjects of tricks designed to satisfy engagement metrics. Amarna Miller says she treats algorithms as any mass media outlet would while prioritizing message over virality; Simó notes two differences from the Dumas and Gerald Brenan era: locals can now correct or parody content, and some local creators adopt clichés because they reap algorithmic reward. David Diaz of Minor Hotels says more than 60% of guests are inspired by social media to travel (ev4), noting specialized creators generate greater audience retention and bookings while journalists affect brand image.

The article closes with Boggs's advice — research, learn the language, and don't assume everything is cheap — alongside Dickmann's warm take on Murcia, including observations about 'The Sidewalk Phalanx' and devotion to El Corte Inglés. The evidence line ev3 references Minor Hotels having more than 84 establishments in Spain but does not connect that figure to a chartable quantity or comparison basis within the text, so it is excluded from any visual.
items.title: American Influencers Reshape How Spaniards See Themselves Through Foreign Eyes

items.summary:
France 24 correspondents examine Japan's radical left in the 1970s, when several movements turned to armed struggle and violent action. The team met with two former militants more than half a century after these events.

In the late 1960s, amid student and worker unrest, a small group of far-left activists founded the Red Army Faction and went underground while being hunted by police. Some took refuge in central Japan's mountains around 1971 to prepare for armed struggle under the name United Red Army; however, internal purges claimed their own members first, with 12 activists executed during self-criticism sessions that turned into lynchings.

The Asama Lodge incident followed: a hostage-taking and 10-day siege broadcast live on Japanese television. The event traumatised the public and marked the end of the revolutionary student movement in Japan.

Meanwhile, the struggle continued abroad with a second group based in Lebanon to support the Palestinian cause, which took the name Japanese Red Army. It was led by Fusako Shigenobu, known as the 'Red Queen,' who spent many years in prison. Members were notably responsible for the 1972 attack on Tel Aviv Airport, which left 26 people dead.

FRANCE 24's Alexis Bregère, Mélodie Sforza, Ayana Nishikawa and Aruna Popuri reported.
items.title: Japan's radical past: Retracing the far-left groups of the 1970s

items.summary:
In the coastal fishing town of Kayar, Senegal, families continue to lose loved ones at sea even as poverty and limited opportunities push young people toward a dangerous journey across the Atlantic in search of Europe. Falla Dionne has not heard from her husband since he left for Spain in July 2022; their three-month-old son was with him when the boat reportedly never reached shore, according to accounts relayed by those who waited nearly a month for news before being told the vessel had failed to arrive.

Despite such losses, others remain determined. Fisherman Baye Coura Diop has attempted the crossing three times and once spent 15 days at sea; he said God intervened each time but that he intends to set out again if God wills it. His mother, Sally Ndiaye, says she no longer tries to stop him from leaving.

She attributed his departures to poverty and young people's desire to support their families through compassion for their parents, praying only that God guide them safely so the family can help one another. Senegal's struggling fishing industry, rising living costs, and limited job opportunities are cited as factors driving these departures.

Even with increased European funding for border surveillance and efforts to intercept migrant boats, thousands continue to risk the dangerous Atlantic crossing toward Spain's Canary Islands, leaving families in Kayar increasingly faced with a choice between staying without prospects or risking everything for a better future.
items.title: Senegalese migrants risk deadly Atlantic crossing from coastal town of Kayar

items.summary:
Guinea-Bissau's military leadership has defended its decision to postpone the presidential and legislative elections originally planned for next month until November 2028. Transitional president General Horta N'Tam said on Thursday that conditions were not in place to hold the polls, breaking from the one-year transition to civilian rule promised after last year's coup. The presidency stated an assessment of electoral preparations found insufficient technical, material, and financial conditions to organize a credible vote.

N'Tam described the country as being assured at all levels in its current special context, citing preserved relations with bilateral and multilateral partners and behavior marked by civility and respect for authorities. He characterized the transition record to date as positive while noting reforms require more time and resources than initially planned. A nationwide electoral census would be needed under a new division of constituencies reduced from 29 to 12, and parliament membership would fall from 102 to 65 members.

The elections are now scheduled for November 26, 2028, three years after the generals came to power. The military coup on November 26, 2025 occurred just before provisional results were due in an election held three days earlier that ousted President Umaro Sissoco Embalo and suspended the electoral process. Regional bloc ECOWAS had called for a short, structured, and transparent transition back to civilian rule after his removal.

The military government held a constitutional referendum in August replacing the semi-parliamentary structure with strengthened presidential powers, though opposition groups called for a boycott of that vote. Many observers suspected Embalo orchestrated the 2025 coup to halt an election process he appeared to be losing, while recent steps suggest the current leadership is distancing itself from him. Guinea-Bissau has experienced four previous coups and attempted coups since gaining independence from Lisbon in 1974.
items.title: Guinea-Bissau military government defends postponing elections

items.summary:
Gérard Depardieu, France's most celebrated actor for decades, was ordered Thursday by the Paris Court of Appeal to stand trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting a young actress. The ruling came less than two weeks after he abandoned his appeal against a separate sexual assault conviction.

Actress Charlotte Arnould accused 77-year-old Depardieu in 2018 of raping her at his Paris home when she was 22. On Aug. 7, the court ruled that he should face trial over allegations from an incident on that date while dismissing claims relating to a second occurrence six days later. The decision upholds part of investigating judge's August 2025 order to send Depardieu to trial.

Depardieu has denied the rape allegations and disputes Thursday's ruling, according to his lawyer Delphine Meillet, who did not specify whether he would challenge it before France's highest court for civil and criminal cases. The case is described as one of the most prominent in France's reckoning with sexual violence amid resistance to the #MeToo movement.

The controversy intensified after a December 2023 television documentary showed Depardieu making obscene remarks during a 2018 trip to North Korea, prompting French President Emmanuel Macron to defend him and invoke the presumption of innocence. In November 2016, he abandoned his appeal against a conviction for sexually assaulting two women on a film set in 2021, accepting an 18-month suspended prison sentence and issuing a public apology.

Depardieu was convicted in May 2025 of groping a set decorator and an assistant during the filming of 'Les Volets Verts' ('The Green Shutters'), with the court ordering his name listed in France's national sex offender database. The case has drawn comparisons to earlier cultural resistance, including a 2018 open letter signed by actress Catherine Deneuve and 99 other women defending men's freedom to make advances toward women.
items.title: French Actor Gérard Depardieu Ordered to Stand Trial on Rape and Sexual Assault Charges

items.summary:
Election day arrived in Victoria after a campaign marked by falling Labor polling and a last-minute Coalition policy dump, with around half of the state's 4.7 million eligible voters having already voted through postal ballots and early voting centres while the remainder headed to polling booths.

The election is widely expected to end 12 years of Labor rule, though the Coalition's path relies on winning more than a dozen new seats amid rising One Nation support. Both parties endured leadership turmoil since their 2022 victories: Daniel Andrews resigned in 2023 before Jacinta Allan took over and later stepped down amid Big Build corruption allegations, Ben Carroll then became leader after a chaotic party room meeting; meanwhile the Liberals cycled through three leaders—Matthew Guy, Brad Battin, and Jess Wilson—who stabilized as the opposition surged on law-and-order messaging.

One Nation is expected to attract more than 20 per cent of the primary vote despite tempered recent polls, while Greens leader Ellen Sandell warned her party faces tough hurdles because preference deals mean a seat win requires outpacing Labor, Liberal, and One Nation combined. The ABC will provide election night coverage from 6pm across its TV channels, iview, radio stations including 774 ABC Melbourne, and online platforms.

The article notes the campaign extended well beyond traditional six-week timeframes with no leaders debate but a televised forum featuring Carroll, Wilson, One Nation's Warren Pickering, and Greens' Ellen Sandell. Labor braced for an historically low primary vote amid soaring debt and Big Build allegations, while Coalition candidates faced controversies including social media posts praising Adolf Hitler, anti-Muslim rhetoric, sexualized remarks about consent, misogynistic comments involving former AFL player Dustin Martin, and leader Warren Pickering admitting a history of drug use and drink driving.
items.title: Victoria's Election Day Arrives as Coalition Poised to Oust Labor

items.summary:
The Adani Group is seeking government approval to invest in India's airline sector, according to group CFO Jugeshinder 'Robbie' Singh speaking at the Trust India Debt Capital Market Summit 2026. The move forms part of a wider expansion plan requiring substantial funding, with group companies expected to borrow ₹1.3-1.4 trillion annually over FY27 and FY28 while also raising capital from domestic and international markets.

Singh said more than 60 crore people in India have the potential to fly, meaning daily flights would need to rise nearly tenfold to 30,000 to meet demand. He requested government permission at least to allow investment so that Adani could fund airlines directly or support other airline companies and entrepreneurs entering the space.

The group has stated it can invest ₹4.5-5 trillion annually from a capital standpoint, with EBITDA expected to triple over five years, though Singh noted execution capability is constrained by infrastructure ecosystem limitations. It has committed to investing $120 billion over the next five years, with annual capex rising from ₹80,000 crore three years ago to ₹1.1 trillion and then ₹1.56 trillion in subsequent years.

Singh indicated Adani Airports would be operationally ready for a demerger rather than an IPO by calendar year 2027, potentially creating a separate listed entity. The airport business was established as a subsidiary of Adani Enterprises after the group won concessions to operate six airports and has since expanded its portfolio to eight with Navi Mumbai International Airport.

On financials, Singh said net borrowings would increase by only around $25 billion over five years despite debt repayments of $25-30 billion even as EBITDA triples. He added aggregate credit quality had improved from A-/BBB+ levels in 2018-19 to AA+ currently.

Data centres are emerging as another major investment area, with the group having drawn down $900 million against an existing $3 billion financing arrangement and overall funding agreements expected to reach around $10 billion over four years. Adani Airport Holdings' non-aeronautical revenue share is currently around 60% and nearing its targeted range of 60-65%. The group, founded by Gautam Adani in 1988, has grown into a diversified infrastructure conglomerate with 13 listed companies spanning energy, utilities, ports, airports, roads, cement, metals and media.

The article was written by Subhana Shaikh, a business journalist at Mint who covers the Reserve Bank of India, monetary policy, and India's bond markets. She has seven years of experience reporting on financial markets with a focus on banking and the broader financial system.
items.title: Adani Group Seeks Approval to Invest in Airlines

items.summary:
Adani Group Chief Financial Officer Singh told reporters in Mumbai that he wished well for the Tatas, describing them as a 'storied' group when asked about recent developments within the conglomerate. He said the Adani Group wanted every Indian company to expand and hoped domestic businesses would eventually account for half of the Fortune 500 list, adding that 'the Adani Group wants every Indian corporate to grow.'

These remarks come ahead of the November 30 Tata Sons board meeting, where differences between Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata and the company's management center on Chandrasekaran's proposed reappointment for a third five-year term and the holding company's listing. The Reserve Bank of India has mandated a public listing of Tata Sons after classifying it as an upper-layer non-banking financial company (NBFC), while Noel Tata has proposed restructuring it as an operating company to avoid that requirement.

At the September 17 board meeting, four directors backed Chandrasekaran's continuation, including Tata Trusts nominee Venu Srinivasan, while Noel Tata was the sole dissenter.
items.title: Adani CFO Comments on Tata Group Amid Board Dispute

items.summary:
Meta-owned WhatsApp announced on November 26 that users will be able to buy and install travel eSIM plans directly within the app, partnering with several telecom operators and eSIM providers. The named partners include India's Reliance Jio, Smart Axiata, Smart Communications, and Verizon, though WhatsApp is also working with additional carriers and providers to expand availability.

The feature aims to let travellers obtain mobile internet abroad without purchasing a local SIM card or paying for international roaming plans. Users reportedly can complete the purchase and installation in just a few steps while continuing to use their existing WhatsApp number for messages and calls, since an eSIM is described as a digital SIM that does not require inserting a physical card.

WhatsApp has stated the service will roll out in select countries soon but has not confirmed whether India will be among the first markets. The company also has not disclosed which partners will provide network coverage across different regions or explain how those arrangements work.

Several details remain unspecified, including plan pricing, data allowances, and active durations. WhatsApp head Kunal Shah posted on X about the feature as an early step toward offering eSIM services and invited more operators and providers to join. The article notes that using the service will require a smartphone compatible with eSIM technology, and whether it becomes cheaper for Indian travellers depends on its eventual availability and pricing once further details are shared.
items.title: WhatsApp Partners With Reliance Jio for International Travel eSIMs

items.summary:
Uttar Pradesh's Jaunpur police have suspended constable Vinay Shankar for his role in planning and executing a gold robbery in Lucknow. The accused, a 2019-batch constable posted at the Line Bazaar police station who originally hails from Rae Bareli, was reportedly fond of a lavish lifestyle with around 1.34 lakh Instagram followers, used a latest-model iPhone, owned a Royal Enfield Shotgun motorcycle, and lived in a relationship with a woman constable.

The robbery occurred on the night of November 21 near an HP petrol pump in Khurdahi Bazaar, Sushant Golf City, Lucknow. Two police constables and a Directorate of Revenue Intelligence official posed as policemen to stop a bus carrying gold trader Mahendra Das, who was returning from Jaunpur after delivering jewellery there on November 20; the group robbed him around 1:30 am in a white Swift Dzire before handing over the stolen goods to associates. Police have arrested five accused while several others, including Vinay Shankar, remain absconding.

Jaunpur superintendent of police Dr Yashveer Singh said departmental action had been initiated against the constable and that he was suspended as the investigation into the robbery continued.
items.title: Jaunpur constable suspended over Lucknow gold robbery

items.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India reduced the minimum daily maintenance requirement for the cash reserve ratio (CRR) from 99 percent to 90 percent, effective from the fortnight beginning December 1, 2026. The central bank cited an assessment of current and evolving macroeconomic conditions and liquidity conditions in its notification. This relaxation follows a period during which overnight rates rose above the policy corridor.

The decision comes as system liquidity slipped into deficit for the first time since June 22. According to RBI data, the liquidity deficit widened to Rs 47,641.20 crore on November 26 from Rs 32,216 crore a day earlier. Pressure was also evident in Friday's operations: banks submitted bids worth Rs 1.35 lakh crore at the three-day variable rate repo auction against Rs 75,000 crore offered. The weighted average call rate stood at 5.76 percent on Friday, above the marginal standing facility rate of 5.75 percent.

In October, when liquidity was in surplus following the FCNR-B deposit scheme, the RBI had raised the minimum daily CRR maintenance requirement from 90 percent to 99 percent while keeping the overall CRR unchanged at 3 percent. The central bank noted that this shift reflects changing conditions as it moved between easing and tightening its cash reserve requirements.
items.title: RBI Eases Daily CRR Maintenance To 90% As Banking Liquidity Slips Into Deficit

Sanjay Malhotra, Governor of the Reserve Bank of India, said on Friday that only about 20 to 30 per cent of eligible Indian exports take advantage of lower tariffs under free trade agreements (FTAs), while partner countries' exports into India use those benefits at a rate of roughly 60 to 70 per cent. He made the remarks at the SME Finance and Investment Summit, describing the gap as an opportunity being left on the table and urging firms to learn about FTAs relevant to their products.

Malhotra noted that India has signed numerous FTAs over the past five years with countries including the UAE, Australia, the UK and New Zealand, some of which are not yet operationalised. He said these agreements give enterprises access to new markets, lower-cost quality inputs and niche global value-chain segments, though he stressed that capitalising on them depends critically on timely and adequate finance.

The governor highlighted the size of India's MSME sector, saying it accounts for about 31 per cent of GDP, 35 per cent of manufacturing output and nearly half of merchandise exports, while providing livelihoods to more than 45 crore people. He added that this sector was essential to post-pandemic growth above 7.4 per cent.

Malhotra said raising MSME productivity toward the levels seen in advanced economies could generate gains equivalent to 11 per cent of GDP. He also encouraged firms to diversify financing beyond bank loans through equity, venture capital, leasing and factoring, and urged adoption of artificial intelligence, which he estimated could create $490-685 billion in economic value for the sector even though only about 5 per cent of MSMEs use it actively.
items.title: RBI Governor Says Only 20-30% Of Eligible Indian Exports Use FTA Benefits

In East Singhbhum district of Ranchi, a couple was arrested on November 27, 2026, over allegations that they killed their 14-year-old daughter and disposed of her body. Ravindra Murmu and his wife Sumani Murmu are accused of striking Kanaklata Murmu, a Class VIII student from Layadih village under Kamalpur police station limits, on the head with a stick during an argument over her Instagram use on November 10.

East Singhbhum SP (Rural) Shubham Kumar Khandelwal said the couple allegedly dumped Kanaklata's body in a deep, water-filled abandoned stone quarry that night and later claimed she had gone missing. The remains were recovered from the quarry on November 13, prompting police to register an FIR against unidentified persons on November 14 based on a statement given by the girl's father.

Police reportedly questioned several villagers and gathered technical evidence over the following 10 days after the parents' conduct raised suspicion. During subsequent questioning, both accused allegedly confessed to the crime before being arrested and remanded to judicial custody. Police stated that further investigation into the incident was underway.
items.title: Couple Arrested for Allegedly Killing Daughter Over Instagram Use in Jharkhand

items.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has cut the minimum daily maintenance requirement for its cash reserve ratio (CRR) from 99% to 90%, effective from the fortnight beginning December 1, 2026. The central bank said it made the decision based on an assessment of current and evolving macroeconomic conditions and liquidity. Under the new directive, scheduled banks must maintain at least 90% of their prescribed CRR each day during the reporting fortnight, though the average maintained over the entire period must still meet RBI's requirement.

The move reverses a change introduced just over a month earlier when the central bank raised the minimum daily maintenance requirement from 90% to 99%, effective October 16, 2026. The reduction lowers only the minimum daily threshold without changing the prescribed CRR rate itself; for example, at a CRR of 4.5%, banks must deposit Rs 4.50 with the RBI for every Rs 100 of deposits, leaving Rs 95.50 available for lending and other operations.

RBI said the change gives scheduled banks greater flexibility to manage day-to-day liquidity by holding a smaller proportion of required reserves on individual days while still meeting the fortnightly average requirement.
items.title: RBI Lowers Minimum Daily CRR Maintenance Requirement to 90%

Swaminathan J, Deputy Governor of the Reserve Bank of India, addressed the 31st meeting of the Standing Advisory Committee in Kolkata on November 27, 2026, urging banks to expedite credit sanctions and reduce reliance on collateral through cash-flow-based lending via ULI and other digital channels. He recognised micro, small and medium enterprises' contribution to India's economy and development goals while calling for greater use of the Trade Receivables Discounting System (TReDS) for receivables financing and early identification and resolution of stress.

The Deputy Governor also invited industry associations to participate in RBI town halls and district-level MSME SAMVAAD meetings to raise members' concerns with banks. The committee reviewed working capital and investment credit, lending to first-time borrowers, collateral-free lending limits, settlement of CPSE invoices through TReDS, and key provisions of the MSMED (Amendment) Act, 2026.

Meanwhile, RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra said Indian exporters, particularly MSMEs, are not fully leveraging free trade agreement benefits. He reported that only about 20-30 per cent of eligible exports were availing tariff concessions compared with the 60-70 per cent utilisation by partner countries exporting to India.

The meeting was attended by officials from the Ministry of MSME and Department of Financial Services, bank executives, heads of SIDBI, NABARD, CGTMSE, NCGTC and KVIC, the CEO of the Indian Banks' Association, and representatives of national, regional and state-level MSME associations.
items.title: RBI Deputy Governor Urges Banks to Speed Up MSME Credit

DMK chief MK Stalin accused the Tamil Nadu government led by the TVK alliance of bringing disgrace to the state after it failed to mount a strong defence before the Supreme Court in the Deepam case. His remarks came hours after the court observed that the authorities were prima facie in contempt for defying its order, and he posted on X that 'the incompetent TVK government has brought unprecedented peril to Tamil Nadu,' calling the verdict in the Thiruparankundram matter a blatant defeat.

Stalin said the Supreme Court's directives—handing over security of the temple and hill to the CRPF, suspending its board of trustees, appointing two former judges to oversee management, and summoning senior officials—constituted a shock. He argued that state rights secured by the Dravidian movement were being surrendered to the Union government through this single legal case, likened the TVK handling to 'a monkey mishandling a delicate flower garland,' and blamed chief minister C Joseph Vijay's lack of experience for his silence, which Stalin called a historic betrayal.

The court order followed authorities' failure to permit the ceremonial lighting of the Karthigai Deepam lamp atop the Deepathoon in Madurai despite a one-time directive issued on November 20. Instead, the lamp was lit at its customary spot near the Ucchi Pillayar temple's Deepa Mandapam.
items.title: Stalin Blames TVK Government for Disgrace After Supreme Court Rebuke in Deepam Case

Days before a special parliamentary session, the government withdrew the original Delimitation Bill, 2026 from the Lok Sabha and introduced its replacement, titled the Delimitation (Second) Bill, 2026. The withdrawal was announced in a statement signed by minister of state for law and justice Arjun Ram Meghwal on November 27.

The revised legislation provides for a 50 per cent increase in seats allocated to each state and Union Territory in the Lok Sabha and their legislative assemblies, while also giving effect to women's reservation. Women's reserved seats would be allotted through rotation as decided by the Delimitation Commission, with that quota running for 15 years from the commencement of the 2023 amendment.

The original Bill had been introduced on April 16 alongside two related bills to set up a Delimitation Commission and redraw constituency boundaries. The accompanying Constitution Amendment Bill failed to secure the special majority required under Article 368 when put to consideration on April 17, so those measures were not pursued further.

The revised version requires the Centre to constitute the Delimitation Commission as soon as possible after it comes into force rather than from time to time. It also directs use of latest census figures published on that date, meaning the 2011 Census would apply if no newer figures are released before enactment. The government said the uniform increase would enhance overall representation while preserving the existing relative distribution of seats among states.
items.title: Government Replaces Delimitation Bill With Revised Version

Union Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said on Friday that the pathway to a trade deal with the United States is taking 'some shape' and has come close to culmination. The comments followed two days after the US proposed fresh tariffs of up to 25% on Indian products following an investigation into alleged excess production, along with levies of varying rates on goods from 13 other economies including China and the European Union.

The new tariffs against India would be reduced to 17% once New Delhi and Washington sign a formal trade agreement. The Office of the Trade Representative said these duties would replace rather than add to the existing 10% tariffs, and the levies are subject to public comment before taking effect under Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act.

Goyal also stated that a free trade agreement with the European Union will come into effect by March or April. On November 15 he had said the US would offer Indian goods preferential trade access and lower import duties than those imposed on competing countries under the proposed deal. After an interim trade deal agreed on February 2, tariffs on Indian goods were set to fall to 18% from a combined rate of 50%, which included a punitive levy of 25% imposed in August 2025 over India's purchase of Russian oil.
items.title: India-US Trade Deal Pathway Shaping After New Tariff Proposal

A commentary argues that India's Large Area Certification (LAC) tool, introduced in the 2020-21 fiscal year under the Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana via Participatory Guarantee System-India, offers a low-cost way to formally recognise farmland that has long been chemical-free. The author illustrates this with Budra, a farmer on a hillside in Koraput district of Odisha whose fields have never used synthetic fertiliser and already meet organic standards that farmers elsewhere pay years and thousands of dollars to achieve.

The piece contrasts LAC's recognition model against the dominant global approach: it notes the worldwide organic market is worth around 145 billion euros ($160 billion) annually, according to the annual FiBL-IFOAM survey, and rests largely on an expensive conversion process that requires a two-to-three-year transition window with dipping yields before producers can command premiums. LAC instead verifies historical chemical-free land use at community or block level without a transition period, so it certifies what already exists rather than manufacturing change.

The author points to Dantewada district in Chhattisgarh as the first major mainland trial of LAC, where administration certified 110 villages covering roughly 65,000 hectares and more than 10,000 farmers through a PGS Regional Council rather than individual farm audits. Koraput is presented as the clearest case for applying the policy: in 2012 the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization designated its Jeypore tract a Globally Important Agricultural Heritage System among only about ninety such sites worldwide.

The commentary warns that this heritage faces quiet encroachment from the chemical input economy, with local traders extending credit-tied seed and fertiliser packages to commercial hybrid crops while seasonal migration leaves older farmers short of labour on steep slopes. It argues Koraput should adopt LAC as a natural completion of Odisha's Millets Mission, which has built procurement and demand for rainfed grains but left the certified organic premium unclaimed because the soil remains uncertified.

The author concludes that certifying an intact baseline costs almost nothing today, whereas waiting until chemicals have taken hold would incur full conversion costs including lost income, dead soils needing restoration, retrained farmers, and large public subsidies. For Koraput, Large Area Certification is framed as a cost-effective way to protect the agricultural heritage before it degrades permanently.
items.title: India's overlooked policy could help recognise chemical-free farmland

The Nationalist Congress Party (Sharadchandra Pawar) faction announced it will support the delimitation bill in Parliament, according to party leader Jitendra Awhad. Speaking on Friday after a discussion with party chief Sharad Pawar, Awhad said the conversation was not about an official stance but that the general point made was that delimitation is a constitutional requirement and 'a decision has been made to support the delimitation process.' The faction's eight Lok Sabha MPs and one Rajya Sabha member will back it after the party issued a whip directing its members to attend Parliament's special session beginning Monday. Awhad gave this statement hours after the Union Cabinet cleared the fresh bill, which reportedly proposes increasing Lok Sabha seats in all states by 50% (ev1), maintaining seat proportions based on the 1971 census (dt2), and freezing that arrangement for another 25 years until 2051. Details of the bill were not immediately available at press time.

The NCP group had voted against a similar delimitation package in April, when it failed to secure the two-thirds majority required for constitutional amendments because the ruling National Democratic Alliance lacks such numbers in either House (ev4). The draft legislation introduced that month also sought to raise Lok Sabha strength from 543 to 815 and operationalize the 33% women's reservation quota, which was brought into force on April 16. Opposition INDIA bloc members argue population-based delimitation would give northern and central states an undue advantage over southern states, where population growth has been better controlled, while Congress leader Rahul Gandhi alleged it could allow the BJP to 'gerrymander' seats for its benefit in the 2029 elections (dt7). The government has not disclosed the agenda for the special session.
items.title: NCP Sharadchandra Pawar Faction to Support Delimitation Bill

The Constitution 132nd Amendment Bill 2026, signed by Union Law Minister Arjun Ram Meghwal, proposes a one-third reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies through delimitation. The bill includes separate categories for Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe women, with seat rotation managed by Parliament over a period of 15 years.

The legislation also calls for a 50 percent increase in seats across these legislatures. The maximum strength of the House of the People would rise to 815 members from states and 35 from union territories, while state assemblies could expand up to 650 members.

The Union Cabinet has approved amendments to both the Delimitation and Women Reservation Bills ahead of a special session of Parliament reconvening on November 30.
items.title: Constitution 132nd Amendment Bill Proposes Women Reservation and Expanded Seats

UCADA lost track of the aircraft on its monitoring system as it crossed the Joshimath valley, according to authority chief executive Prateek Jain, who told the Press Trust of India that UCADA subsequently grounded Trans Bharat's entire fleet while the Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau investigates.

items.summary: The Securities and Exchange Board of India has granted approval to the proposed public issue by Ananya Birla-led Svatantra Microfin. The draft filing describes a fresh equity share offering aggregating up to Rs 1,500 crore alongside an offer for sale of up to Rs 1,500 crore by existing shareholders, with the new shares set to be listed on both the BSE and NSE (ev1, ev2). Svatantra Microfin plans to use net proceeds from the fresh issue mainly to strengthen its Tier I capital base in line with anticipated growth-driven lending needs. Chaired by Ananya Birla as a non-executive director linked to the Aditya Birla Group legacy, the lender was the first institution granted the NBFC-MFI licence introduced by the Reserve Bank of India in 2011 (dt3). Beyond microfinance loans, it offers secured products such as affordable housing finance and loans against property through its subsidiary Svatantra Micro Housing Finance Corporation. The company ranked second-largest among Indian NBFC-MFIs by microfinance assets under management across March 31, 2024, 2025, and 2026 (dt4). Between FY24 and FY26 it was the fastest-growing peer in that category, posting a compound annual growth rate of 20.87% as microfinance AUM rose from Rs 14,437.87 crore to Rs 21,093.22 crore (ev7, ev8). Amid elevated credit costs and asset-quality pressures in FY25 and FY26, Svatantra Microfin reported the lowest Gross Stage 3 ratio among peers at 2.24% and 1.19%, respectively (ev12, ev13), along with peer-leading return on average AUM of 2.90% in FY25 and 3.57% in FY26, plus returns on equity of 13.66% and 15.00% over the two years (ev14, ev15, ev16, ev17). As of March 31, 2026 its microfinance operations spanned 2,123 branches across 20 states and 394 districts, supported by 24,594 employees including 15,575 field officers serving 4.27 million active borrowers (ev18). Axis Capital, Avendus Capital, IIFL Capital Services, Kotak Mahindra Capital Company, and SBI Capital Markets are acting as book running lead managers for the issue.

Historian Edward Anderson argues that diaspora Hindu nationalism is neither a pure import from India nor an entirely independent abroad phenomenon, but rather a two-way exchange in which money flows mainly to India while messaging moves both directions. He published his study of these transnational networks in 2024 after years of fieldwork among Hindu organizations in Britain and beyond.

On financial flows, Anderson says the evidence points overwhelmingly from the diaspora to India through registered charities; Bellingcat reported that two US charities linked to the movement received $117.8 million between 2020 and 2024, much of it granted abroad chiefly to projects in India. He notes family remittances move substantial sums but are nearly invisible to researchers, while US political action committees represent Indian American money rather than funds from India.

Anderson describes how the direction of organization has shifted since 2014, when the Indian state and BJP became more active patrons of the diaspora through stadium spectacles and groups like the Overseas Friends of the BJP. He cites a BBC finding that more than half of about 200,000 tweets about the 2022 Leicester unrest originated in India as evidence that much online content now flows outward from India.

On impact and limits, Anderson cautions against claiming Hindu nationalism itself has become mainstream; rather it is a set of claims made in the name of 'the Hindu community' by organizations whose ideological commitments many politicians do not fully understand. He adds caveats that anti-Indian hostility in the US has genuinely risen during Trump's second term and that the flow runs both ways, with Romila Thapar suggesting minority experiences abroad shape majority mentality.

Anderson also highlights resistance within the diaspora from Dalit and Ambedkarite organizers who have advanced caste on the legal agenda, as well as progressive Hindu voices. He notes surveys suggest Modi support is lower and more divided in Britain than in the US, while recent polling indicates Reform UK support among British Indians has risen sharply since 2024 despite a low base.
items.title: Edward Anderson on Diaspora Hindutva's Money and Messaging

A 60-year-old woman was sexually assaulted and struck on the forehead inside an unmanned washroom at Ghatkopar railway station late Thursday night, according to reports. She had finished work as a daily wager and traveled with her 18-year-old daughter before going into the washroom around 11:12 pm.

CCTV footage captured a man in his twenties entering shortly after she went inside; police said he locked the door from within, assaulted her in the passage, then left at 11:19 pm heading toward Ghatkopar Metro. She informed her daughter around 11:22 pm, and they approached the Government Railway Police desk on platform no. 4 for help.

The accused was identified as Taslim Noor Mohammad after police traced him to Asalpha in Ghatkopar using CCTV leads; authorities are now checking whether he has a prior crime history. A rape case was registered under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, and several teams were formed to locate him.

The incident is being described as highlighting security lapses at suburban railway stations.
items.title: Man Arrested After Sexually Assaulting Woman in Mumbai Railway Washroom

Chief of Defence Staff General NS Raja Subramani warned on Friday (November 27) that Pakistan's advancing space programme, backed by strategic support from China and Türkiye, poses a new threat to India's national security. Speaking at the Vivekananda International Foundation in Delhi during a session moderated by former CDS General Anil Chauhan, he said Islamabad's growing orbital reach demands an urgent upgrade to New Delhi's own space-based military infrastructure.

Subramani cautioned that defence ties among Beijing, Islamabad, and Ankara — which became more visible during last year's Operation Sindoor — mean Chinese satellite networks will directly benefit Pakistan. He stated that whatever intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance, positioning, navigation, and timing capability China has available would become accessible to Pakistani forces.

To counter this, he said India must accelerate Phase III of its Space Based Surveillance mission. Spearheaded by the Defence Space Agency, the Rs 26,968-crore initiative aims to deploy 52 dedicated military satellites over three years through a joint effort between ISRO and private-sector firms.

Beyond orbital security, Subramani observed that the boundary separating conflict from peacetime is eroding, leaving nations in what he called a 'continuous state of contestation.' Without naming specific actors, he warned adversaries are targeting India through cognitive warfare. Citing Operation Sindoor as an example of integrated multi-domain combat, he emphasized technological superiority remains transitory and urged India to develop its own strategic template rather than follow foreign blueprints.
items.title: India's CDS warns of Pakistan space alliance with China and Türkiye

items.summary:
The Union Cabinet on Friday approved the Delimitation (Second) Bill, 2026, a constitutional amendment aimed at implementing reservation of seats for women in Parliament and state legislative assemblies. The bill proposes a uniform increase of 50 per cent in Lok Sabha seats allocated to each state and union territory as well as in the total number of assembly seats.

According to a copy of the Bill accessed by Hindustan Times, if enacted the government will constitute a delimitation commission that would carry out the exercise on the basis of the last published census. The bill does not explicitly mention a fixed proportion or a freeze on each state's share, and it was passed after the earlier 131st Amendment Bill faltered in the Lok Sabha on April 17 with 298 votes in favour against 230.

The previous attempt sought to raise the seat ceiling from 543 members to a maximum of 850, comprising up to 815 seats from states and 35 from union territories. The bill also aimed to implement reservation for women ahead of the 2029 polls. Union home minister Amit Shah had offered a uniform rise in every state's seats as part of last-minute talks before the united Opposition blocked the measure.

Critics argued that allocating all 850 seats by population on the 2011 Census could reduce southern states' share, even though South India contributes around 30-31 per cent of GDP. The government responded that every state's seats would rise by the same proportion to address these concerns.

Because the NDA does not hold a two-thirds majority required for constitutional amendments on its own, any fresh attempt will depend on neutral parties and fence-sitters, with each vote and absence counting toward passage.
items.title: India approves delimitation bill to raise Lok Sabha strength and reserve women's seats
